body_markdown:
If you’re Metro Detroit car folk, you may have encountered the Miyamoto Volkswagen at a car show or engaged it in a traffic-signal contest. It’s been on the street for over 40 years, and it’s a machine one doesn’t soon forget. Aside from 18.5-inch-wide rear gums that are visible only from under the rear bumper, some air ducting, and a windup key on the trunk, this ’72 Bug appears to be nothing more than an old VW that’s still creeping along. Even the wheels look stock. But pull up next to it at a stoplight in your muscle car or exotic, and do a little flexing, and you’re likely to get your doors blown off. Should you pull into a parking lot afterward and ask the VW’s driver what kind of potent force lurks under the hood, he’ll likely turn a switch that activates a motor and hydraulic pump, and that conventional VW body will rise[like that of a funny car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/lessons-learned-from-a-six-year-stint-building-nitromethane-funny-car-engines/) to reveal a stout steel chassis, 572-cubic-inch rat motor, and full rollcage.


At a glance, perhaps when sitting next to you at a traffic light, the Miyamoto VW appears to be nothing more than an old Bug in nice condition.


Paul Stenquist


From the rear, the VW’s windup key mocks; the big rubber under the rear fenders is a warning.


Paul Stenquist


Ernie Miyamoto is the current owner and caretaker of the angry little Beetle, having taken over shepherding of the mind-blowing machine from his brother some twenty years ago. The Miyamotos are car people. Ernie remembers how, more than half a century ago, he and his brother, Larry, then toddlers, would ride in the back seat of one of the family’s numerous Hemi-powered Mopars as their dad, San Miyamoto, and their uncle cruised the streets of Waterford and Pontiac looking for a street race and a payday.


Way back then, San was a skilled machinist at a tool-and-die shop in the Detroit area, a top-drawer technician, racer, and all-around automotive enthusiast. After a couple decades of muscle-car fun, San, in 1985, decided he wanted to build a Volkswagen hot rod. “Can’t be done,” his pals told him. “Of course it can,” he answered and set out to do it. He purchased a ’72 VW and discarded just about everything, save the body. Then he built a stout frame of 2×3-inch steel rails that would run the length of the car, front to rear. Atop those rails, he constructed a cage of 1.5-inch steel tubing. Both frame rails and the roll cage were of 1/8-inch wall thickness. The chassis was more than sturdy enough to handle big horsepower, and thanks to its diminutive dimensions, the car would still be a lightweight.


San Miyamoto purchased this ’72 VW body in 1984. It would soon become one of the fastest, most powerful VWs to roam the planet.


Paul Stenquist


A chassis of rectangular steel rails and steel tubing was constructed to fit within the confines of the Volkswagen body.


Paul Stenquist


For big horsepower, San dropped a 454 cu-in Chevy big block between the frame rails, backed by the stout GM THM400 automatic. Power was delivered via a very short driveshaft to a narrowed Dana 60 rear with 4.10:1 gearing. The wheels were 15-inch VW wheels, so they appeared stock. The rears were, of course, cut, welded, and made much wider for big rubber.


The narrowed Dana 60 rear is dwarfed by the 18.5-inch-wide rear tire and the Ernie Miyamoto–fabricated 3-inch exhaust pipes.


Paul Stenquist


As San worked, his son, Ernie, who was now in his early twenties, would pitch in from time to time. Ernie was busy with his own project as well—a ’67 Nova hot rod—but he found time to help with various chores of framing and fabricating the Volkswagen.


San enjoyed the car for a good number of years but eventually moved on to other things. San’s younger son, Larry, drove and maintained the VW for a time, and eventually passed it on to his brother, Ernie, who has been updating the car and enjoying it for the last couple of decades.


Vents in the hood pass air to the radiator and allow engine-compartment heat to exit.


Paul Stenquist


Today, the Miyamoto VW sports a Chevrolet Performance 572 cu-in crate engine. That monster knocks out 672 horsepower and 645 lb-ft of torque. Ernie has applied some spit and polish here and there, to keep the old Bug looking good. A new front suspension from Heidts provided a substantial handling upgrade. The tires have been upgraded over the years, but they’re still mounted on VW wheels, and all are branded Mickey Thompson. The rears measure 31 inches in diameter with 18.5 inches of tread. The front tires are 26 inches in diameter and six inches wide.


The hood can be opened to allow access to the engine with the body lowered. The 572 cu-in Chevy crate motor knocks out 621 horsepower, a bit more than your typical Volkswagen engine.


Paul Stenquist


The red upholstered passenger cabin offers a gear selector, comfortable seating, and a full complement of gauges.


Paul Stenquist


The hydraulic cylinders are tucked in behind the seats. They can easily hold the body open or keep it tightly closed. Latches are unnecessary.


Paul Stenquist


Heidts front suspension provides excellent wheel control and a comfortable ride.


Paul Stenquist


San Miyamoto is now well into his ninth decade and is taking it easy, but he’s still a car guy. His main ride is a restored[Checker cab](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/100-years-ago-checkers-kalamazoo-factory-produced-its-first-taxicab/) that he drives on road trips with the[Classic Legends car club](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/classic-legends-is-a-detroit-car-club-on-the-move/) .


Meanwhile, Ernie has been busy building his automotive fabrication business. Today, his MotoFab shop in Davisburg, Michigan, is a leading supplier of hot rods and race cars. An expert fabricator, he does a lot of header and exhaust system work, along with complete builds and restorations. On the VW, Ernie’s custom pipes route the exhaust from the Vee-Dub’s big Chevy to the rear of the machine. The nonfunctional stock VW exhaust pipes remain in place, as they’re part of the show. Many Motor City hot rodders have looked with despair at those itty-bitty pipes. The VW’s windup key mocks, but the big rubber under the rear fenders is a warning.


Sitting next to you at a stoplight, the Miyamoto machine appears to be nothing more than an old, nicely kept VW with a goofy windup key on the back. The push of a switch on the dash drastically alters the picture.


Paul Stenquist


From most angles, the VW appears to be nothing more than an old Bug with some holes in the hood. Or is that the frunk?


Paul Stenquist


Paul Stenquist
